opus-5.5.text:
Well, one of the things that's really striking is that almost everything we know about how children learn comes from the laboratory. We bring a child in, we give them a carefully designed little machine — a box that lights up when you put certain blocks on it, say — and we see what they do. And what we've found is that even very young children are remarkably good at the kinds of things scientists do: they figure out causal structure, they pay special attention to evidence that's surprising or confounded, and they play in ways that seem designed to resolve that uncertainty.

But the big question is, what does that look like out in the wild? When a two-year-old is in the kitchen pulling every pot out of the cabinet and banging them together, or dropping the spoon off the high chair for the fifteenth time, is that the same kind of systematic experimentation we see in the lab? My suspicion is that it is — that what looks to grown-ups like getting into everything is actually a kind of exploration that's tuned to exactly the information the child needs. But we don't really know, because nobody has had a good record of what children's everyday experience actually looks like from their point of view.

So with head-mounted cameras you can start to ask: How much of a child's day is spent in this kind of exploratory play? How varied is it? When they encounter something surprising, do they go back and test it again, the way they do in our experiments? Do they vary what they do in a way that's actually informative, rather than just random?

And there's a second reason this is interesting right now, which is the comparison with AI. Large language models learn from this enormous body of text, essentially passively. Children get a tiny fraction of that data, and yet they end up understanding the world in a much more robust way. A big part of the answer, I think, is that children aren't just passively absorbing data — they're actively going out and generating the data themselves, by experimenting. If we could actually characterize what that self-generated curriculum looks like, the specific things children do to learn about the world, that might tell us something deep about human intelligence, and maybe even how to build systems that learn more like children do rather than like very large, very well-read librarians.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether children repeat tests after surprising events and whether their actions are informative, but it does not clearly propose analyzing the experiential outcomes that follow those actions.

r002.rationale: It says everyday behavior that looks like “getting into everything” may actually be exploration tuned to the information children need, and compares it to systematic lab experimentation.

r003.rationale: It describes children actively experimenting to generate data themselves and learn about the world.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the thing that's always struck me is that there's this enormous gap between what we see in the lab and what children are actually doing out in the world. In the lab, we give a child a little machine, the "blicket detector," and we see that they can figure out how it works, that they'll do the right experiments to find the cause. And that's wonderful, but it's a very constrained situation. What I'd really want to know from the GoPro recordings is: how much of a child's ordinary day is actually taken up with something that looks like experimentation?

My guess, and it's really only a guess, is that it's a lot more than we think. When you watch a two-year-old at a dinner table, dropping the spoon over and over, pushing the cup to the edge, that looks a lot like a systematic exploration of the physics of the situation, even though the parents experience it as the child being annoying. So the first thing is just a kind of natural history. What are the objects they go after? Do they go after the ones that are surprising, the ones that violate their expectations, the way we see in controlled studies? And is there a structure to it, where they try one thing, see what happens, and then vary it, the way a good experimenter would?

The second thing, which I think is actually deeper, is the social side. Almost everything a child learns, they learn in the presence of other people. So I'd want to see how much of the experimenting is really a kind of joint activity, where the child does something, looks at the caregiver, the caregiver reacts, and that reaction itself becomes data. And the other way around: how often is the child watching what adults do and then testing it? We know from the lab that children are quite sophisticated about this, that they'll imitate more when they think the adult is knowledgeable, less when they think the adult is just fooling around. But we have no idea what the base rates look like in a real kitchen or a real playground.

And then there's a methodological point that I find exciting. The reason I've gotten interested in talking to the AI people is that these recordings give you something like the actual training data of a human child. If you want to know what kind of learner could produce a four-year-old, you need to know what they actually see and do, not what we imagine they see and do. The old view was that the input is impoverished and so the knowledge has to be built in. The recordings let you check that directly. My suspicion is that the input turns out to be much richer, and much more actively shaped by the child, than that story assumes. Children aren't passive recipients of a data stream. They're going out and generating the data they need, and that's exactly what a good scientist does.

r001.rationale: The response proposes tracking what draws a child to an object, what the child does with it, and what happens next, including whether the child varies the action.

r002.rationale: It suggests that behavior adults may see as annoying is actually systematic exploration, and asks whether children vary their actions like experimenters.

r003.rationale: It describes repeated actions such as dropping a spoon as exploration of the situation’s physics, aimed at learning how the world works.

astra-6.text:
What I’d really like to know is how much of what children do in everyday life has the structure of an experiment. If you watch a two-year-old, they’re constantly getting into things, repeating things, changing things slightly. And from an adult’s perspective, that can look like aimless activity, or like they’re deliberately trying to drive you crazy. But it could be a very effective way of finding out how the world works.

In the lab, we can give children a little machine and show that they’ll systematically explore it to figure out what makes it go. The question is whether they do that spontaneously, when there isn’t a psychologist presenting them with a puzzle. Do they try something, get a surprising result, and then change what they do in a way that helps them distinguish between possible explanations?

The recordings would let us look at that sequence from the child’s perspective. We could see what information was actually available to them, what they chose to investigate, and what happened next. And we could begin to ask whether the things we call play are, in fact, a kind of everyday experimental science.

r001.rationale: The response proposes examining what information was available before an investigation, what the child did, and what happened next, including surprising results that prompt a change in action.

r002.rationale: It suggests apparent aimless activity may be effective investigation and asks whether children spontaneously explore in ways that distinguish explanations.

r003.rationale: It says children’s everyday activity may be a way of finding out how the world works.

sol-6.1.text:
What I’d really like to know is how much of what children do in everyday life is actually experimentation. When you watch a child in a laboratory, you can show that they’re very sensitive to evidence, that they’ll try things out to distinguish between different hypotheses. But we’ve set up the situation for them. We’ve decided what the problem is and what the relevant possibilities are.

The much more interesting question is, how do they decide what to investigate in the first place? If you watch a two-year-old wandering around the house, opening drawers and putting things into things, it can look terribly random. But perhaps there’s a structure to it. Perhaps they do something, get a surprising result, and then vary what they do next in a way that helps them figure out what happened.

The recordings would let us look for those sequences in ordinary life, without an experimenter directing the child’s attention. And they’d let us see what evidence children actually have available to learn from. We know a lot about what children eventually understand, but much less about the everyday experiences that get them there.

r001.rationale: It proposes looking for sequences in ordinary life: a child does something, gets a surprising result, then varies the next action to figure out what happened.

r002.rationale: It says apparently random behavior may have structure and describes children varying actions in response to results.

r003.rationale: It proposes that children investigate to understand surprising outcomes and learn from everyday experience.
